terms.grammar: construction: the length of time in the accusative, with no preposition
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.40: inediam bīduum aut trīduum ferunt
terms.comment: Only with words of time (hōram, diem, bīduum, annum). A distance or a thing is not a length of time: “he slept the whole journey” is per tōtum iter dormīvit, not tōtum iter. Age is said the same way: decem annōs nātus.

evidence: Liv. 22.2.7: per quadrīduum jam et trēs noctēs
terms.comment: Stresses that it lasted the whole time; see also during.

terms.gloss: for (a time ahead: what is meant to last)
evidence: Ter. Eun. 191: in hoc bīduum, Thāis, valē
terms.comment: “For tomorrow”, in crāstinum; “for ever”, in perpetuum.

phrases.latin: nam mihi ante oculōs diēs noctēsque versāris
phrases.english: for you are before my eyes day and night

phrases.latin: aniculae saepe inediam bīduum aut trīduum ferunt
phrases.english: little old women often go without food for two or three days

phrases.latin: mustum sī volēs tōtum annum habēre, in amphoram mustum inditō et corticem oppicātō, dēmittitō in piscīnam. post diēs XXX eximitō. tōtum annum mustum erit
phrases.english: if you want grape juice all year, put the juice in a jar, pitch the cork and sink it in the pond; take it out after thirty days; there will be grape juice all year

phrases.latin: captō cibō ac pecoribus per trīduum exercitum aluit
phrases.english: with the food and the flocks he had captured he fed the army for three days

phrases.latin: In hoc bīduum, Thāis, valē. — Mī Phaedria, et tū; numquid vīs aliud?
phrases.english: Goodbye for these two days, Thais. — And you, my Phaedria; is there anything else?

phrases.latin: cētera intēctī tōtōs diēs jūxtā focum atque ignem agunt
phrases.english: otherwise unclothed, they spend whole days by the hearth and the fire
